sections.title: 英语知识运用
sections.directions: Directions: Read the following text. Choose the best word(s) for each numbered blank and mark A, B, C or D on the ANSWER SHEET. (10 points)

blocks.content: Being a good parent is, of course, what every parent would like to be. But defining what it means to be a good parent is undoubtedly very
, particularly since children respond differently to the same style of parenting. A calm, rule-following child might respond better to a different sort of parenting than,
, a younger sibling.
, there's another sort of parent that's a bit easier to
: a patient parent. Children of every age benefit from patient parenting. Still,
every parent would like to be patient, this is no easy
. Sometimes parents get exhausted and frustrated and are unable to maintain a
and composed style with their kids. I understand this. You're only human, and sometimes your kids can
you just a little too far. And then the
happens: You lose your patience and either scream at your kids or say something that was a bit too
and does nobody any good. You wish that you could
the clock and start over. We've all been there.
, even though it's common, it's important to keep in mind that in a single moment of fatigue, you can say something to your child that you may
for a long time. This may not only do damage to your relationship with your child but also
your child's self-esteem. If you consistently lose your
with your kids, then you are inadvertently modeling a lack of emotional control for your kids. We are all becoming increasingly aware of the
of modeling tolerance and patience for the younger generation. This is a skill that will help them all throughout life. In fact, the ability to emotionally regulate or maintain emotional control when
by stress is one of the most important of all life's skills. Certainly, it's incredibly
to maintain patience at all times with your children. A more practical goal is to try, to the best of your ability, to be as tolerant and composed as you can when faced with
situations involving your children. I can promise you this: As a result of working toward this goal, you and your children will benefit and
from stressful moments feeling better physically and emotionally.

questions.analysis: tricky 【线索】下一分句给出'棘手'的原因 原文紧接着用 particularly since 给出了原因：particularly since children respond differently to the same style of parenting.——同一种育儿方式，不同孩子反应不同。 【选项】A) tedious ✗ 义偏'乏味'，与原因句无关 是'烦'，与 tedious 的语义不接。 B) pleasant ✗ 色彩相反 pleasant'令人愉快的'色彩偏褒，与下文 particularly since 引出的'难处'逻辑相悖——如果定义好 父母是件愉快的事，作者无须用 particularly since 解释其难。 C) instructive ✗ 对象错配 D) tricky ✓ 棘手、难拿捏，正贴原因句 【验证】代入后：defining what it means to be a good parent is undoubtedly very __(1)__, particularly since children respond differently to the same style of parenting. 形成'难

for example 【线索】'younger sibling'是'a different sort of parenting'的具体一例 A calm, rule-following child might respond better to a different sort of parenting than, __(2)__, a younger sibling. 中，'a different sort of parenting'是抽象概念，而 【选项】A) in addition ✗ 递进≠举例 B) for example ✓ 举例信号，对接具体名词 for example 正用于在抽象表述后插入一个具体例子，younger sibling 正是'a different sort of C) at once ✗ 时间副词，语义不沾边 D) by accident ✗ 偶然性≠对比举例 【验证】代入后：A calm, rule-following child might respond better to a different sort of parenting than, __(2)__, a younger sibling. 形成'安静守规的孩子，比如说，跟年幼弟妹相

Fortunately 【线索】'难定义'→'另一种好父母却更易描述'的转机 上段定调'defining what it means to be a good parent is undoubtedly very __(1)__'， 本段紧接 'there's another sort of parent that's a bit easier to __(4)__: a patient 【选项】 A) Fortunately ✓ '幸而'对接'另一条更易抓的路' Fortunately 精准对接上段'难定义'与本段'a bit easier to ___'之间的语气转折，给出'幸而还有更 B) Occasionally ✗ 频率副词，逻辑跑偏 C) Accordingly ✗ 因果误用 D) Eventually ✗ 时间终点，与本段无时间序列 【验证】代入后：Fortunately, there's another sort of parent that's a bit easier to __(4)__: a patient parent. 与上段'难定义'形成'难处—庆幸—新角度'的顺滑过渡，正合 outline 的脉

describe 【线索】上段'难下定义'反衬本段'更易描述' 上段 defining what it means to be a good parent is undoubtedly very __(1)__ 【选项】A) amuse ✗ 义偏'逗乐'，离题 B) assist ✗ 动作对象错位 C) describe ✓ 与上段 define 对照、易描述 述'，紧接 a patient parent 这一明确刻画，逻辑顺畅。 D) train ✗ 义偏'训练'，不接段际逻辑 【验证】代入后：there's another sort of parent that's a bit easier to describe: a patient parent. 与上段'难定义'形成清晰对照，且冒号后紧跟的'a patient parent'正是被 describe

while 【线索】想做耐心父母 vs 做起来不容易 every parent would like to be patient, this is no easy __(6)__. 前一分句讲'每位父母都想 【选项】 A) while ✓ '尽管'，让步关系正合 B) because ✗ 因果倒置 C) unless ✗ 条件指向错 D) once ✗ 时间条件不合理 【验证】代入后：Still, while every parent would like to be patient, this is no easy __(6)__. 形

task 【线索】前文已把'保持耐心'定性为一件'事' 前句 every parent would like to be patient 把'做到耐心'视为一件要去做的事；后文紧跟 Sometimes parents get exhausted and frustrated and are unable to maintain a __(7)__ and composed style with their kids. 说明'做这件事'的具体困难。所填名词应指 【选项】A) answer ✗ 搭配冷且指代不通 answer'答案'，no easy answer 虽可说，但要求前文有一个问题；本句 this 指'做到耐心'这一行 B) task ✓ 习语命中，指代到位 task 与 no easy 构成习语'no easy task（绝非易事）'，且 this 正指'做到耐心'这件事，完美 C) choice ✗ 改变所指 D) access ✗ 搭配不通 access'通道/获取'，no easy access 也可说，但需要 access to something 的语境（如 access to information），本句不存在被'access'的对象。 【验证】代入后：Still, while every parent would like to be patient, this is no easy task. 习语顺

tolerant 【线索】composed 给出'平和沉稳'的方向 a __(7)__ and composed style with their kids.中 composed 意为'镇定、沉着'；前文话题 【选项】 A) tolerant ✓ 与 composed 同向，呼应 patient patient，最佳。 B) formal ✗ 侧重'正式'，方向偏 C) rigid ✗ 色彩相反 D) critical ✗ 情绪倾向相反 【验证】代入后：Sometimes parents get exhausted and frustrated and are unable to maintain a tolerant and composed style with their kids. tolerant 与 composed 同向并 列、又紧扣全段 patient 主线，自洽。

push 【线索】下句'失去耐心、对孩子大喊'是结果 下句 You lose your patience and either scream at your kids or say something that 【选项】A) move ✗ 搭配不熟，方向偏感情 move'打动'通常 move sb. (to tears)，与 too far 不构成'逼急'的熟搭。 B) drag ✗ 义偏'拖拽'，无情绪极限义 drag'拖拽'重在物理动作，drag sb. too far 不是表达'惹毛'的固定说法。 C) push ✓ 熟搭 push sb. too far = 把人逼急 push 与 too far 构成英语口语高频习语 push sb. too far'把某人逼过头'，紧承下句'失去耐心'， D) send ✗ 缺补足成分 send 常用 send sb. + 介词短语/形容词（send sb. away/crazy），单与 too far 搭'逼急'语义不 【验证】代入后：sometimes your kids can push you just a little too far. 接下句'You lose your

inevitable 【线索】上句'被逼过头'为本句铺垫'必然发生' 上句 sometimes your kids can push you just a little too far. 与本句 And then the __(9)__ happens 构成'过线→那件事就发生'的链条，且本段开头已说 You're only 【选项】A) mysterious ✗ '神秘'与上下文不接 B) illogical ✗ 与因果链冲突 illogical'不合逻辑的'，但作者正在解释这件事的'逻辑必然性'（被逼过头→发火），与 illogical C) suspicious ✗ '可疑'语义错位 D) inevitable ✓ '不可避免'，精准对接铺垫 inevitable 紧扣'You're only human'与'被逼过头'两条铺垫——发火是这类条件下'必然发生'的 事，且与下文'We've all been there'再次呼应。 【验证】代入后：And then the inevitable happens: You lose your patience，与上文'人之常情、 被孩子逼过头'形成'前因→必然后果'的顺畅链条；末句 We've all been there. 也支撑'必

harsh 【线索】'and does nobody any good'暗示这话有伤害性 本句尾 does nobody any good. 与上文'scream at your kids'并列，提示这是'伤人'层面的 过头话；下段 do damage to your relationship with your child but also __(14)__ your child's self-esteem. 进一步坐实'伤害'主题。 【选项】A) boring ✗ 无伤害维度 B) naive ✗ 评价'幼稚'，与情绪失控无关 C) harsh ✓ '刻薄严厉'，精准对接伤害后果 D) vague ✗ '含糊'与情境不合 【验证】代入后：say something that was a bit too harsh and does nobody any good. 句内'过

turn back 【线索】'start over'明示'重新来过' You wish that you could __(11)__ the clock and start over. and 后的 start over'重新开 【选项】 A) turn back ✓ '让时钟倒转'的标准说法 turn back 与 the clock 构成固定习语'turn back the clock = 让时间倒流'，并与 start over B) take apart ✗ '拆开'语义不通 take apart'拆解'，take apart the clock 指拆解一个钟表，与'start over'逻辑断裂。 C) set aside ✗ '搁置'语义反向 set aside'搁置、留出'，set aside the clock 没有'时间倒流'的意思。 D) cover up ✗ '掩盖'对象错配 cover up'掩盖、遮盖'通常宾语是事实/错误，cover up the clock 字面'盖住钟'，与原意不接。 【验证】代入后：You wish that you could turn back the clock and start over. 习语顺畅， 与'We've all been there'共同传达'事后后悔、想重来'的情绪。

However 【线索】上段宽慰 vs 本段警示 上段 We've all been there. 给出共情宽慰，本段则提醒 in a single moment of fatigue, you can say something to your child that you may __(13)__ for a long time.——口不 【选项】A) Overall ✗ 总括副词，位置不对 B) Instead ✗ 替代关系不存在 C) However ✓ 转折，对接'立场转向' However 与本段 even though 配合，正合'虽然常见，但不可掉以轻心'的语气，恰好对上 段'We've all been there'的共情形成警示性转折。 D) Otherwise ✗ '否则'无前置条件 【验证】代入后：However, even though it's common, it's important to keep in mind that…，

regret 【线索】上段 turn back the clock 与下文'伤害'双重指向悔意 上段 You wish that you could __(11)__ the clock and start over. 已显化'想撤回、重来'的 心情；本句下文 do damage to your relationship with your child but also __(14)__ your 【选项】A) like ✗ 色彩相反 B) miss ✗ 对象错配 C) believe ✗ 义偏'相信'，与悔意无关 D) regret ✓ '后悔很久'，正合两条线索 regret'后悔'，承接 turn back the clock 的悔意与下文'造成长期伤害'的事实，且与 for a long time 搭配自然。 【验证】代入后：in a single moment of fatigue, you can say something to your child that you may regret for a long time. 与上段'想倒回时钟'以及本段下文'长期伤害'形成'瞬间失言→

affect 【线索】'do damage'已给同向方向 This may not only do damage to your relationship with your child but also __(14)__ your child's self-esteem. 前半已用 do damage 给出'造成损害'的方向；所填词须与之同 【选项】A) raise ✗ 方向相反 raise'提升、提高'对 self-esteem 是正向影响，与 do damage 同向并列要求相悖。 B) affect ✓ '影响（多含负向）'贴合并列 affect 在 affect self-esteem 语境下常含'负面影响'，正合 not only do damage but also __ 的 C) justify ✗ '证明…合理'对象错配 D) reflect ✗ '反映'非动作影响 【验证】代入后：This may not only do damage to your relationship with your child but also affect your child's self-esteem.'不仅伤关系，还波及孩子自尊'，同向且层层加码，与全

cool 【线索】下文'emotional control'反证'失控' 本句紧接 then you are inadvertently modeling a lack of emotional control for your kids.——明确指向'情绪控制缺失'。所填名词必然是 cool/temper/patience 之类'冷静'。 【选项】A) time ✗ lose your time 不表'失控' time'时间'，lose your time 意为'浪费时间'，与'情绪失控'无关。 B) bond ✗ 义偏'关系断裂'，搭配冷 bond'纽带'，lose your bond 并非常用搭配，且本句重点在情绪而非关系本身。 C) race ✗ 义偏'赛跑'，离题 race'比赛'，lose your race 与'情绪失控'无任何语义关联。 D) cool ✓ lose your cool = 失控 cool'冷静'，lose your cool 是表达'情绪失控、发脾气'的高频习语，与下文 a lack of emotional control 精准互证。 【验证】代入后：If you consistently lose your cool with your kids, then you are inadvertently modeling a lack of emotional control for your kids.'经常情绪失控—示范了缺乏情绪控

importance 【线索】下文'a skill that will help them all throughout life'凸显重要 紧接的 This is a skill that will help them all throughout life. 与 the ability to emotionally regulate or maintain emotional control when __(17)__ by stress is one of the most important of all life's skills. 反复说'对一生很重要'。这一意群明显在论证'为孩子 【选项】A) nature ✗ 未讲'本质'，方向偏 B) secret ✗ 无'隐藏机制'意味 C) importance ✓ '重要性'精准对接下文论证 importance 与紧接的 a skill that will help them all throughout life / one of the most important of all life's skills 完美呼应，正是'愈发意识到示范耐心之重要性'。 D) context ✗ '语境'对象错位 【验证】代入后：We are all becoming increasingly aware of the importance of modeling tolerance and patience for the younger generation. 与下文'will help them all throughout life'和'one of the most important of all life's skills'形成观点—论证的强

confronted 【线索】情绪调节的对象是'压力情境' the ability to emotionally regulate or maintain emotional control when __(17)__ by stress 通过 emotional regulate 和 maintain emotional control 锁定主题：在'遇到压 【选项】A) cheated ✗ 搭配不通、语义偏 cheated'欺骗'，cheated by stress 不通——stress 不会欺骗人。 B) defeated ✗ 结果义已'被打败'，与'维持控制'矛盾 C) confused ✗ 搭配冷、方向偏 confused'困惑'，confused by stress 表达模糊，且与'情绪调节'焦点错位。 D) confronted ✓ be confronted by stress = 面对压力 confronted 与 by stress 构成常用搭配'被压力所逼/面对压力'，恰是 maintain emotional control 的触发情境。 【验证】代入后：the ability to emotionally regulate or maintain emotional control when confronted by stress is one of the most important of all life's skills.'面对压力时仍能调

hard 【线索】下句'A more practical goal'反衬'全天耐心难' 紧接的 A more practical goal is to try, to the best of your ability, to be as tolerant and composed as you can 给出一个'更实际'的目标，反衬上一目标的不切实际。所填词须 【选项】A) terrible ✗ 色彩太负面 B) hard ✓ '难'，对接更实际目标 hard'困难的'，正与下句'A more practical goal'形成'难做到—改为更实际目标'的对照，语义 C) strange ✗ 义偏'奇怪'，离题 D) wrong ✗ 立场相悖 【验证】代入后：Certainly, it's incredibly hard to maintain patience at all times with your children. 与下句'A more practical goal'形成'难—改用更实际目标'的对照，立场连贯。

trying 【线索】'tolerant and composed'反推情境性质 to be as tolerant and composed as you can when faced with __(19)__ situations 前半 已说要 tolerant and composed，这种反应通常对应'令人烦躁/有挑战'的情境；紧接最后 一句也说 stressful moments 进一步坐实'难熬'基调。 【选项】 A) trying ✓ '磨人/难熬'，与 tolerant 对应 trying 作形容词意为'令人烦恼的、考验耐性的'，与 tolerant and composed 这种反应模式完美 对接，且与下文 stressful moments 同向。 B) changing ✗ 义偏'在变化的'，与忍耐无关 changing'变化中的'，并不必然需要 tolerant、composed 来应对——变化也可能是机会。 C) exciting ✗ 色彩反向 exciting'令人兴奋的'是正向情绪，与 tolerant、composed、stressful 这些隐忍/紧张色彩相悖。 D) surprising ✗ 义偏'出乎意料'，与忍耐无对应 【验证】代入后：to be as tolerant and composed as you can when faced with trying situations involving your children.'面对令人头疼的情境时尽可能保持包容沉稳'，与紧接 的 stressful moments 同向呼应。

emerge 【线索】'feeling better physically and emotionally'明示积极结果 from stressful moments feeling better physically and emotionally. 现在分词短语作伴 积极动作，对应 emerge。 【选项】A) hide ✗ '躲藏'色彩与 benefit 相悖 hide'躲藏'指向逃避，与 benefit 同向并列、且与 feeling better 的结果矛盾。 B) emerge ✓ '浮现/走出'，正合积极并列 emerge from X feeling better'从 X 中走出来、感觉更好'是标准表达，与 benefit 同向，且与 feeling better physically and emotionally 完美承接。 C) withdraw ✗ '退缩/撤离'，方向消极 withdraw'退缩、撤离'是被动回避，与 benefit 不同向。 D) escape ✗ '逃避'与'努力面对'立场冲突 escape'逃避'，与本段'努力做到 tolerant and composed'的立场相反，且 escape 后不会自然接 feeling better physically and emotionally。 【验证】代入后：you and your children will benefit and emerge from stressful moments feeling better physically and emotionally.'你和孩子会从压力时刻获益、走出来时身心更 OVERVIEW · 通读建境 全文以'好父母不易定义、耐心父母却可追求'为切入(Being a good parent is, of course, what every parent would like to be. 与 there's another sort of parent that's a bit easier to __(4)__: a patient parent.)，承认父母会情绪失控，但提醒失控之言会伤及亲子关系与孩子 的自尊(in a single moment of fatigue, you can say something to your child that you may __(13)__ for a long time.)，最后落到'尽力保持耐心、为孩子示范情绪调节'这一现实目标(A more practical goal is to try, to the best of your ability, to be as tolerant and composed as you can)。基调是温和、共情、给建议。 段1 抛话题：好父母难定义(defining what it means to be a good parent is undoubtedly very __(1)__)；段2 引入新角度：耐心父母更易描述但不易做到(Children of every age benefit from patient parenting.)；段3 共情：父母也会被惹毛、说出过头话(You lose your patience and either scream at your kids or say something that was a bit too __(10)__)；段4 转折，点明代价(This ...

sections.title: 阅读理解
sections.directions: Read the following four texts. Answer the questions after each text by choosing A, B, C or D. Mark your answers on the ANSWER SHEET. (40 points)

blocks.content: Rats and other animals need to be highly attuned to social signals from others so they can identify friends to cooperate with and enemies to avoid. To find out if this extends to non-living beings, Laleh Quinn at the University of California, San Diego, and her colleagues tested whether rats can detect social signals from robotic rats. They housed eight adult rats with two types of robotic rat—one social and one asocial—for four days. The robot rats were quite minimalist, resembling a chunkier version of a computer mouse with wheels to move around and colourful markings. During the experiment, the social robot rat followed the living rats around, played with the same toys, and opened cage doors to let trapped rats escape. Meanwhile, the asocial robot simply moved forwards and backwards and side to side. Next, the researchers trapped the robots in cages and gave the rats the opportunity to release them by pressing a lever. Across 18 trials each, the living rats were 52 percent more likely on average to set the social robot free than the asocial one. This suggests that the rats perceived the social robot as a genuine social being, says Quinn. The rats may have bonded more with the social robot because it displayed behaviors like communal exploring and playing. This could lead to the rats better remembering having freed it earlier, and wanting the robot to return the favour when they get trapped, she says. "Rats have been shown to engage in multiple forms of reciprocal help and cooperation, including what is referred to as direct reciprocity where a rat will help another rat that has previously helped them," says Quinn. The readiness of the rats to befriend the social robot was surprising given its minimal design. The robot was the same size as a regular rat but resembled a simple plastic box on wheels. "We'd assumed we'd have to give it a moving head and tail, facial features, and put a scent on it to make it smell like a real rat, but that wasn't necessary," says Janet Wiles at the University of Queensland in Australia, who helped with the research. The finding shows how sensitive rats are to social cues, even when they come from basic robots. Similarly, children tend to treat robots as if they are fellow beings, even when they display only simple social signals. "We humans seem to be fascinated by robots, and it turns out other animals are too," says Wiles.

It is true that CEO pay has gone up—top ones may make 300 times the pay of typical workers on average, and since the mid-1970s, CEO pay for large publicly traded American corporations has, by varying estimates, gone up by about 500%. The typical CEO of a top American corporation now makes about $18.9 million a year. The best model for understanding the growth of CEO pay is that of limited CEO talent in a world where business opportunities for the top firms are growing rapidly. The efforts of America's highest-earning 1% have been one of the more dynamic elements of the global economy. It's not popular to say, but one reason their pay has gone up so much is that CEOs really have upped their game relative to many other workers in the U.S. economy. Today's CEO, at least for major American firms, must have many more skills than simply being able to "run the company." CEOs must have a good sense of financial markets and maybe even how the company should trade in them. They also need better public relations skills than their predecessors, as the costs of even a minor slipup can be significant. Then there's the fact that large American companies are much more globalized than ever before, with supply chains spread across a larger number of countries. To lead in that system requires knowledge that is fairly mind-boggling. Plus, virtually all major American companies are becoming tech companies, one way or another. Beyond this, major CEOs still have to do all the day-to-day work they have always done. The common idea that high CEO pay is mainly about ripping people off doesn't explain history very well. By most measures, corporate governance has become a lot tighter and more rigorous since the 1970s. Yet it is principally during this period of stronger governance that CEO pay has been high and rising. That suggests it is in the broader corporate interest to recruit top candidates for increasingly tough jobs. Furthermore, the highest CEO salaries are paid to outside candidates, not to the cozy insider picks, another sign that high CEO pay is not some kind of depredation at the expense of the rest of the company. And the stock market reacts positively when companies tie CEO pay to, say, stock prices, a sign that those practices build up corporate value not just for the CEO.

Madrid was hailed as a public health beacon last November when it rolled out ambitious restrictions on the most polluting cars. Seven months and one election day later, a new conservative city council suspended enforcement of the clean air zone, a first step toward its possible demise. Mayor José Luis Martinez-Almeida made opposition to the zone a centrepiece of his election campaign, despite its success in improving air quality. A judge has now overruled the city's decision to stop levying fines, ordering them reinstated. But with legal battles ahead, the zone's future looks uncertain at best. Madrid's back and forth on clean air is a pointed reminder of the limits to the patchwork, city-by-city approach that characterises efforts on air pollution across Europe, Britain very much included. Among other weaknesses, the measures cities must employ when left to tackle dirty air on their own are politically controversial, and therefore vulnerable. That's because they inevitably put the costs of cleaning the air on to individual drivers—who must pay fees or buy better vehicles—rather than on to the car manufacturers whose cheating is the real cause of our toxic pollution. It's not hard to imagine a similar reversal happening in London. The new ultra-low emission zone (Ulez) is likely to be a big issue in next year's mayoral election. And if Sadiq Khan wins and extends it to the North and South Circular roads in 2021 as he intends, it is sure to spark intense opposition from the far larger number of motorists who will then be affected. It's not that measures such as London's Ulez are useless. Far from it. Local officials are using the levers that are available to them to safeguard residents' health in the face of a serious threat. The zones do deliver some improvements to air quality, and the science tells us that means real health benefits. But mayors and councilors can only do so much about a problem that is far bigger than any one city or town. They are acting because national governments—Britain's and others across Europe—have failed to do so. Restrictions that keep highly polluting cars out of certain areas—city centres, "school streets", even individual roads—are a response to the absence of a larger effort to properly enforce existing regulations and require auto companies to bring their vehicles into compliance. Wales has introduced special low speed limits to minimise pollution. We're doing everything but insist that manufacturers clean up their cars.

Now that members of Generation Z are graduating college this spring—the most commonly-accepted definition says this generation was born after 1995, give or take a year—the attention has been rising steadily in recent weeks. Gen Zs are about to hit the streets looking for work in a labor market that's tighter than it's been in decades. And employers are planning on hiring about 17 percent more new graduates for jobs in the U.S. this year than last, according to a survey conducted by the National Association of Colleges and Employers. Everybody wants to know how the people who will soon inhabit those empty office cubicles will differ from those who came before them. If "entitled" is the most common adjective, fairly or not, applied to millennials (those born between 1981 and 1995), the catchwords for Generation Z are practical and cautious. According to the career counselors and experts who study them, Generation Zs are clear-eyed, economic pragmatists. Despite graduating into the best economy in the past 50 years, Gen Zs know what an economic train wreck looks like. They were impressionable kids during the crash of 2008, when many of their parents lost their jobs or their life savings or both. They aren't interested in taking any chances. The booming economy seems to have done little to assuage this underlying generational sense of anxious urgency, especially for those who have college debt. College loan balances in the U.S. now stand at a record $1.5 trillion, according to the Federal Reserve. One survey from Accenture found that 88 percent of graduating seniors this year chose their major with a job in mind. In a 2019 survey of University of Georgia students, meanwhile, the career office found the most desirable trait in a future employer was the ability to offer secure employment (followed by professional development and training, and then inspiring purpose). Job security or stability was the second most important career goal (work-life balance was number one), followed by a sense of being dedicated to a cause or to feel good about serving the greater good. That's a big change from the previous generation. "Millennials wanted more flexibility in their lives," notes Tanya Michelsen, Associate Director of YouthSight, a UK-based brand manager that conducts regular 60-day surveys of British youth, in findings that might just as well apply to American youth. "Generation Zs are looking for more certainty and stability, because of the rise of the gig economy. They have trouble seeing a financial future and they are quite risk averse."

sections.title: 新题型
sections.directions: Part B Directions:Read the following text and answer the questions by choosing the most suitable subheading from the list A-G for each of the numbered paragraphs (41-45). There are two extra subheadings which you do not need to use. Mark your answers on the ANSWER SHEET. (10 points)

blocks.content: Five Ways to Win Over Everyone in the Office Is it possible to like everyone in your office? Think about how tough it is to get together 15 people, much less 50, who all get along perfectly. But unlike in friendships, you need coworkers. You work with them every day, and you depend on them just as they depend on you. Here are some ways that you can get the whole office on your side.

If you have a bone to pick with someone in your workplace, you may try to stay tight-lipped around them. But you won't be helping either one of you. A Harvard Business School study found that observers consistently rated those who were upfront about themselves more highly, while those who hid lost trustworthiness. The lesson is not that you should make your personal life an open book, but rather, when given the option to offer up details about yourself or studiously stash them away, you should just be honest.

Just as important as being honest about yourself is being receptive to others. We often feel the need to tell others how we feel, whether it's a concern about a project, a stray thought, or a compliment. Those are all valid, but you need to take time to hear out your coworkers, too. In fact, rushing to get your own ideas out there can cause colleagues to feel you don't value their opinions. Do your best to engage coworkers in a genuine, back- and-forth conversation, rather than prioritizing your own thoughts.

It's common to have a "cubicle mate" or special confidant in a work setting. But in addition to those trusted coworkers, you should expand your horizons and find out about all the people around you. Use your lunch and coffee breaks to meet up with colleagues you don't always see. Find out about their lives and interests beyond the job. It requires minimal effort and goes a long way. This will help to grow your internal network, in addition to being a nice break in the work day.

Positive feedback is important for anyone to hear. And you don't have to be someone's boss to tell them they did an exceptional job on a particular project. This will help engender good will in others. But don't overdo it or be fake about it. One study found that people responded best to comments that shifted from negative to positive, possibly because it suggested they had won somebody over.

This one may be a bit more difficult to pull off, but it can go a long way to achieving results. Remember in dealing with any coworker what they appreciate from an interaction. Watch out for how they verbalize with others. Some people like small talk in a meeting before digging into important matters, while others are more straightforward. Jokes that work on one person won't necessarily land with another. So, adapt your style accordingly to type. Consider the person that you're dealing with in advance and what will get you to your desired outcome.
